claim: B cells contribute to the pathogenesis of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
source: B cells contribute to the pathogenesis of polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general assertion about B cells' role in PCOS pathogenesis.

claim: The expression level of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) in peripheral blood B cells from PCOS patients was increased.
source: Here, we showed that the expression level of tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) in peripheral blood B cells from PCOS patients was increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including Western blot and flow cytometry results shown in Figure 1.

claim: Metformin used in vitro and in vivo was able to reduce the production of TNF-α in B cells from PCOS patients.
source: Metformin used in vitro and in vivo was able to reduce the production of TNF-α in B cells from PCOS patients.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from in vitro B cell cultures and in vivo patient treatment shown in Figure 2.

claim: Administration of metformin improved mouse PCOS phenotypes induced by dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA).
source: Administration of metformin improved mouse PCOS phenotypes induced by dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and also inhibited TNF-α expression in splenic B cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the DHEA-induced mouse model shown in Figure 7.

claim: Metformin inhibited TNF-α expression in splenic B cells of DHEA-induced PCOS mice.
source: Administration of metformin improved mouse PCOS phenotypes induced by dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) and also inhibited TNF-α expression in splenic B cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from mouse splenic B cells shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Metformin induced metabolic reprogramming of B cells in PCOS patients, including the alteration in mitochondrial morphology.
source: Furthermore, metformin induced metabolic reprogramming of B cells in PCOS patients, including the alteration in mitochondrial morphology, the decrease in mitochondrial membrane potential, Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) production and glucose uptake.
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy images and quantification shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Metformin decreased mitochondrial membrane potential in B cells from PCOS patients.
source: Furthermore, metformin induced metabolic reprogramming of B cells in PCOS patients, including the alteration in mitochondrial morphology, the decrease in mitochondrial membrane potential, Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) production and glucose uptake.
evidence: This is supported by MitoTracker Deep Red flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Metformin decreased ROS production in B cells from PCOS patients.
source: Furthermore, metformin induced metabolic reprogramming of B cells in PCOS patients, including the alteration in mitochondrial morphology, the decrease in mitochondrial membrane potential, Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) production and glucose uptake.
evidence: This is supported by ROS flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Metformin decreased glucose uptake in B cells from PCOS patients.
source: Furthermore, metformin induced metabolic reprogramming of B cells in PCOS patients, including the alteration in mitochondrial morphology, the decrease in mitochondrial membrane potential, Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) production and glucose uptake.
evidence: This is supported by 2-NBDG uptake flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In DHEA-induced mouse PCOS model, metformin altered metabolic intermediates in splenic B cells.
source: In DHEA-induced mouse PCOS model, metformin altered metabolic intermediates in splenic B cells.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 8C-D.

claim: The inhibition of TNF-α expression and metabolic reprogramming in B cells of PCOS patients and mouse model by metformin were associated with decreased mTOR phosphorylation.
source: Moreover, the inhibition of TNF-α expression and metabolic reprogramming in B cells of PCOS patients and mouse model by metformin were associated with decreased mTOR phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing decreased P-mTOR (S2481) in Figures 3 and 8B.

claim: PCOS is one of the most common endocrine-reproductive-metabolic disorder characterized by hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries, and chronic oligo-/anovulation, which can lead to infertility.
source: Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is one of the most common endocrine-reproductive-metabolic disorder characterized by hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries, and chronic oligo-/anovulation, which can lead to infertility (Rotterdam ESHRE/ASRM-Sponsored PCOS consensus workshop group, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Rotterdam consensus criteria.

claim: PCOS occurs under chronic inflammation, leading to ovarian dysfunction and metabolic disorders.
source: Accumulating evidence indicates that PCOS occurs under chronic inflammation, leading to ovarian dysfunction and metabolic disorders (Hu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hu et al., 2020.

claim: Inflammation in PCOS is characterized by elevated levels of inflammatory cytokines (e.g. tumor necrosis factor-alpha [TNF-α], interleukin-6 [IL-6], interferon-γ [IFN-γ]) in the serum, follicular fluid, and ovary.
source: Such inflammation is characterized by elevated levels of inflammatory cytokines (e.g. tumor necrosis factor-alpha [TNF-α], interleukin-6 [IL-6], interferon-γ [IFN-γ]) in the serum, follicular fluid, and ovary (Qin et al., 2016; Xiong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Qin et al., 2016 and Xiong et al., 2011.

claim: CD3+CD4+ T cells of follicular fluid produce high levels of IFN-γ and IL-2 in women with PCOS.
source: Published results have reported that CD3+CD4+ T cells of follicular fluid produce high levels of IFN-γ and IL-2 in women with PCOS and splenic macrophages release more TNF-α in rats with PCOS (Figueroa et al., 2012; Qin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Figueroa et al., 2012 and Qin et al., 2016.

claim: Splenic macrophages release more TNF-α in rats with PCOS.
source: Published results have reported that CD3+CD4+ T cells of follicular fluid produce high levels of IFN-γ and IL-2 in women with PCOS and splenic macrophages release more TNF-α in rats with PCOS (Figueroa et al., 2012; Qin et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Figueroa et al., 2012 and Qin et al., 2016.

claim: Pathologic cytokine-producing B cells have been verified to play important roles in chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, such as diabetes mellitus, multiple sclerosis, and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
source: In chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, such as diabetes mellitus, multiple sclerosis, and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), pathologic cytokine-producing B cells have been verified to play important roles in these diseases (Arkatkar et al., 2017; Jagannathan et al., 2010; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arkatkar et al., 2017; Jagannathan et al., 2010; Li et al., 2015.

claim: In a mouse model of SLE, IL-6 production by B cells drives autoimmune germinal center formation and accelerates disease progression.
source: In a mouse model of SLE, IL-6 production by B cells drives autoimmune germinal center formation and accelerates disease progression (Arkatkar et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arkatkar et al., 2017.

claim: B cells expressing IFN-γ inhibit Treg cell differentiation and exacerbate autoimmune experimental arthritis.
source: B cells expressing IFN-γ inhibit Treg cell differentiation and exacerbate autoimmune experimental arthritis (Olalekan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Olalekan et al., 2015.

claim: The peripheral proportion and activity of CD19+ B cells were increased in women with PCOS.
source: Our previous studies demonstrated that the peripheral proportion and activity of CD19+ B cells were increased in women with PCOS and dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA)-induced morphological changes to mouse ovaries were prevented by CD19+ B cell depletion (Xiao et al., 2019), demonstrating that CD19+ B cells contribute to the pathogenesis of PCOS.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Xiao et al., 2019).

claim: Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA)-induced morphological changes to mouse ovaries were prevented by CD19+ B cell depletion.
source: Our previous studies demonstrated that the peripheral proportion and activity of CD19+ B cells were increased in women with PCOS and dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA)-induced morphological changes to mouse ovaries were prevented by CD19+ B cell depletion (Xiao et al., 2019), demonstrating that CD19+ B cells contribute to the pathogenesis of PCOS.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work (Xiao et al., 2019).

claim: Metformin is a widely used oral medication to treat type 2 diabetes (T2D).
source: Metformin is a widely used oral medication to treat type 2 diabetes (T2D) and also involved in other pharmacological actions, including antitumor effect, antiaging effect, and neuroprotective effect (Bai and Chen, 2021; Bharath et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bai and Chen, 2021; Bharath et al., 2020.

claim: Metformin is involved in other pharmacological actions, including antitumor effect, antiaging effect, and neuroprotective effect.
source: Metformin is a widely used oral medication to treat type 2 diabetes (T2D) and also involved in other pharmacological actions, including antitumor effect, antiaging effect, and neuroprotective effect (Bai and Chen, 2021; Bharath et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bai and Chen, 2021; Bharath et al., 2020.

claim: Metformin not only reduces chronic inflammation through reducing hyperglycemia and increasing insulin sensitivity, but it also has direct anti-inflammatory effects.
source: Published results have suggested that metformin not only reduces chronic inflammation through reducing hyperglycemia and increasing insulin sensitivity, but it also has direct anti-inflammatory effects.
evidence: This is stated as a general assertion based on published results.

claim: Metformin reduces Th17 cytokine production in older subjects.
source: For example, it has been shown that metformin reduces Th17 cytokine production in older subjects (Bharath et al., 2020), decreases the proinflammatory late/exhausted memory B cell subset, and B cell TNF-α mRNA expression in obesity and T2D patients (Diaz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bharath et al., 2020.

claim: Metformin decreases the proinflammatory late/exhausted memory B cell subset in obesity and T2D patients.
source: For example, it has been shown that metformin reduces Th17 cytokine production in older subjects (Bharath et al., 2020), decreases the proinflammatory late/exhausted memory B cell subset, and B cell TNF-α mRNA expression in obesity and T2D patients (Diaz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Diaz et al., 2017.

claim: Metformin decreases B cell TNF-α mRNA expression in obesity and T2D patients.
source: For example, it has been shown that metformin reduces Th17 cytokine production in older subjects (Bharath et al., 2020), decreases the proinflammatory late/exhausted memory B cell subset, and B cell TNF-α mRNA expression in obesity and T2D patients (Diaz et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Diaz et al., 2017.

claim: The effects of metformin are thought to be mediated primarily through regulation of the activity of adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK), the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR), and phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K).
source: The effects of metformin are thought to be mediated primarily through regulation of the activity of adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK), the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR), and phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K), which are major regulators of metabolic stress responses.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about metformin's mechanism of action.

claim: AMPK, mTOR, and PI3K are major regulators of metabolic stress responses.
source: The effects of metformin are thought to be mediated primarily through regulation of the activity of adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK), the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR), and phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K), which are major regulators of metabolic stress responses.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Metformin suppresses systemic autoimmunity in Roquinsan/san mice through inhibiting B cell differentiation via regulation of AMPK/mTOR signaling.
source: Metformin suppresses systemic autoimmunity in Roquinsan/san mice through inhibiting B cell differentiation via regulation of AMPK/mTOR signaling (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2017.

claim: Metformin inhibits the proliferation of rheumatoid arthritis fibroblast-like synoviocytes via inhibiting mTOR phosphorylation through PI3K/AKT signaling.
source: Metformin inhibits the proliferation of rheumatoid arthritis fibroblast-like synoviocytes via inhibiting mTOR phosphorylation through PI3K/AKT signaling (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2019.

claim: Metformin alleviates the aging-associated Th17 inflammation by improving mitochondrial bioenergetics, and reducing oxidative stress via lowering ROS production.
source: Recent evidence has suggested that metformin alleviates the aging-associated Th17 inflammation by improving mitochondrial bioenergetics, and reducing oxidative stress via lowering ROS production (Bharath et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bharath et al., 2020.

claim: Metformin is widely used among women with PCOS and reduces insulin resistance, increases ovulation and improves clinical pregnancy outcomes.
source: At present, metformin is also widely used among women with PCOS and reduces insulin resistance, increases ovulation and improves clinical pregnancy outcomes (Morley et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Morley et al., 2017.

claim: The level of TNF-α was higher in women with PCOS compared to control subjects.
source: Results showed that the level of TNF-α was higher in women with PCOS (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by serum TNF-α measurements shown in Figure 1A.

claim: B cells isolated from PB of women with PCOS expressed higher amounts of TNF-α protein than those from the controls.
source: The results showed that B cells isolated from PB of women with PCOS expressed higher amounts of TNF-α protein than those from the controls (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The percentage of TNF-α+ cells in CD19+ B cells was notably higher in women with PCOS than that in control subjects.
source: We also quantified TNF-α expression in B cells after stimulation with B cell-targeted activator (CpG, CD40L plus anti-IgM/IgA/IgG) by flow cytometry and found that the percentage of TNF-α+ cells in CD19+ B cells was notably higher in women with PCOS than that in control subjects (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: More TNF-α was secreted into the culture supernatants by B cells from women with PCOS compared to controls.
source: More TNF-α was secreted into the culture supernatants (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) is solely secreted by granulosa cells (GCs) of the pre-antral and small antral ovarian follicles.
source: Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) is solely secreted by granulosa cells (GCs) of the pre-antral and small antral ovarian follicles, and could be an effective indicator for the diagnosis of PCOS (Teede et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Teede et al., 2019.

claim: AMH could be an effective indicator for the diagnosis of PCOS.
source: Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) is solely secreted by granulosa cells (GCs) of the pre-antral and small antral ovarian follicles, and could be an effective indicator for the diagnosis of PCOS (Teede et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Teede et al., 2019.

claim: The percentage of TNF-α+ cells in CD19+ B cells was positively associated with serum AMH levels.
source: We analyzed the relationship between the percentage of TNF-α+ cells in B cells and the level of serum AMH by Pearson's correlation analysis, and the results showed that the percentage of TNF-α+ cells in CD19+ B cells was positively associated with serum AMH levels (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by Pearson's correlation analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: TNF-α significantly increased the expression of IL-6, IL-8, CCL2, and CCL20 mRNAs in granulosa cells.
source: We found that TNF-α could significantly increase the expression of IL-6, IL-8, CCL2, and CCL20 mRNAs in GCs (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Metformin significantly inhibited TNF-α production in PCOS-derived B cells in vitro.
source: The results showed that metformin significantly inhibited TNF-α production in PCOS-derived B cells (Figure 2A–B), but did not affect proliferation and apoptosis of B cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Metformin did not affect proliferation and apoptosis of B cells from PCOS patients.
source: The results showed that metformin significantly inhibited TNF-α production in PCOS-derived B cells (Figure 2A–B), but did not affect proliferation and apoptosis of B cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by CFSE proliferation and apoptosis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Metformin's effect on TNF-α production occurred post-transcriptionally because there was no significant change in TNFA mRNA levels.
source: These changes occurred post-transcriptionally because there was no significant change in TNFA mRNA levels (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data showing no change in TNFA mRNA shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The treatment of metformin significantly diminished the expression of TNF-α in B cells from PCOS patients after oral administration for 1 month.
source: Furthermore, we analyzed the expression level of TNF-α in pathological B cells before and after oral metformin for 1 month in PCOS patients. In line with the in vitro results, the treatment of metformin significantly diminished the expression of TNF-α in B cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from patient samples before and after metformin treatment shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The phosphorylation level of AMPK (S487) in CD19+ B cells isolated from PB of women with PCOS was significantly lower compared with control subjects.
source: The results showed that the phosphorylation level of AMPK (S487) in CD19+ B cells isolated from PB of women with PCOS was significantly lower but the phosphorylation levels of PI3K p85 (Tyr458) and mTOR (S2481) were significantly higher compared with control subjects (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The phosphorylation levels of PI3K p85 (Tyr458) and mTOR (S2481) in CD19+ B cells from women with PCOS were significantly higher compared with control subjects.
source: The results showed that the phosphorylation level of AMPK (S487) in CD19+ B cells isolated from PB of women with PCOS was significantly lower but the phosphorylation levels of PI3K p85 (Tyr458) and mTOR (S2481) were significantly higher compared with control subjects (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A, C-D.

claim: Metformin significantly increased the phosphorylation level of AMPK (S487) in B cells from women with PCOS in vitro.
source: In the in vitro culture system of B cells, metformin significantly increased the phosphorylation level of AMPK (S487), and inhibited the phosphorylation levels of PI3K p85 (Tyr458) and mTOR (S2481) in B cells from women with PCOS (Figure 3E–H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3E-F.

claim: Metformin inhibited the phosphorylation levels of PI3K p85 (Tyr458) and mTOR (S2481) in B cells from women with PCOS in vitro.
source: In the in vitro culture system of B cells, metformin significantly increased the phosphorylation level of AMPK (S487), and inhibited the phosphorylation levels of PI3K p85 (Tyr458) and mTOR (S2481) in B cells from women with PCOS (Figure 3E–H).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3E, G-H.

claim: After oral metformin treatment, the phosphorylation level of mTOR (S2481) in peripheral blood B cells from women with PCOS was significantly reduced.
source: After oral metformin treatment, the phosphorylation level of mTOR (S2481) in peripheral blood B cells from women with PCOS was also significantly reduced (Figure 3I–J).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data from patient samples before and after metformin treatment shown in Figure 3I-J.

claim: Oligomycin A, an oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) inhibitor, significantly inhibited TNF-α production in CD19+ B cells isolated from PB of women with PCOS.
source: Oligomycin A, an oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) inhibitor, significantly inhibited TNF-α production in CD19+ B cells isolated from PB of women with PCOS, indicating that the level of OXPHOS in B cells affects the production of TNF-α (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The level of OXPHOS in B cells affects the production of TNF-α.
source: Oligomycin A, an oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) inhibitor, significantly inhibited TNF-α production in CD19+ B cells isolated from PB of women with PCOS, indicating that the level of OXPHOS in B cells affects the production of TNF-α (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is inferred from the effect of oligomycin A on TNF-α production shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Augmented tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and OXPHOS activation in stimulated B cells suggests a coordinated change in mitochondrial dynamics and morphology.
source: Augmented tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle and OXPHOS activation in stimulated B cells suggests a coordinated change in mitochondrial dynamics and morphology (Waters et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Waters et al., 2018.

claim: The majority of mitochondria in metformin-treated B cells became round and the mitochondrial inner membrane disappeared.
source: The results showed that the majority of mitochondria in metformin-treated B cells became round and the mitochondrial inner membrane disappeared (Figure 4B–C), but the mitochondrial numbers were not affected (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy images and quantification shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Metformin did not affect mitochondrial numbers in B cells from women with PCOS.
source: The results showed that the majority of mitochondria in metformin-treated B cells became round and the mitochondrial inner membrane disappeared (Figure 4B–C), but the mitochondrial numbers were not affected (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of mitochondrial numbers shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Metformin decreased MT Deep Red fluorescence intensity and MMP in B cells from women with PCOS.
source: The results showed that metformin decreased MT Deep Red fluorescence intensity and MMP in B cells, suggesting metformin inhibited mitochondrial activity of B cells from women with PCOS (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by MitoTracker Deep Red flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Metformin inhibited mitochondrial activity of B cells from women with PCOS.
source: The results showed that metformin decreased MT Deep Red fluorescence intensity and MMP in B cells, suggesting metformin inhibited mitochondrial activity of B cells from women with PCOS (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is inferred from the decrease in MMP shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Metformin had no effect on mitochondrial mass in B cells from women with PCOS.
source: However, metformin had no effect on mitochondrial mass (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by MitoTracker Green flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: ROS production is considered to be a biomarker of mitochondrial respiration.
source: In addition, ROS production is considered to be a biomarker of mitochondrial respiration.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Excessive ROS can induce oxidative stress, ultimately causing mitochondrial dysfunction and Th17 cytokine production.
source: Excessive ROS can induce oxidative stress, ultimately causing mitochondrial dysfunction and Th17 cytokine production (Bharath et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bharath et al., 2020.

claim: Metformin reduced ROS levels in B cells from women with PCOS.
source: Metformin reduced ROS levels in B cells, suggesting that metformin might behave as an antioxidant to inhibit the expression of proinflammatory cytokines in pathological B cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by ROS flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Metformin might behave as an antioxidant to inhibit the expression of proinflammatory cytokines in pathological B cells.
source: Metformin reduced ROS levels in B cells, suggesting that metformin might behave as an antioxidant to inhibit the expression of proinflammatory cytokines in pathological B cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is speculated based on the reduction in ROS levels shown in Figure 4G.

claim: B lymphocytes rapidly increase glucose uptake following B cell antigen receptor crosslinking.
source: B lymphocytes rapidly increase glucose uptake following B cell antigen receptor crosslinking (Doughty et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Doughty et al., 2006.

claim: The addition of metformin to the B cell culture medium significantly inhibited the uptake of 2-NBDG by B cells from women with PCOS.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, the addition of metformin to the B cell culture medium significantly inhibited the uptake of 2-NBDG by B cells, suggesting that metformin affects the production of TNF-α, which may be related to the inhibition of the energy metabolism by metformin in pathological B cells.
evidence: This is supported by 2-NBDG flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Metformin affects the production of TNF-α, which may be related to the inhibition of the energy metabolism by metformin in pathological B cells.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, the addition of metformin to the B cell culture medium significantly inhibited the uptake of 2-NBDG by B cells, suggesting that metformin affects the production of TNF-α, which may be related to the inhibition of the energy metabolism by metformin in pathological B cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the inhibition of glucose uptake shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Metformin significantly inhibited the expression of glucose transporter Glut 1 and Glut 4 in B cells from women with PCOS.
source: Western blot results showed that metformin significantly inhibited the expression of glucose transporter Glut 1 and Glut 4 in B cells (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: Metformin mainly inhibited the expression of Glut 4 on B cells after a short period of incubation (only 30 min), which had no obvious effect on Glut 1.
source: Furthermore, we found that metformin mainly inhibited the expression of Glut 4 on B cells after a short period of incubation with B cells (only 30 min), which had no obvious effect on Glut 1 (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: Metformin mainly inhibited the expression of Glut 1 rather than Glut 4 on B cells after 4 hr incubation.
source: While metformin mainly inhibited the expression of Glut 1 rather than Glut 4 on B cells after 4 hr incubation (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: HIF1α and c-Myc promote the transcription of metabolic-related genes, including glucose transporters.
source: It was reported that HIF1α and c-Myc promote the transcription of metabolic-related genes, including glucose transporters (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: Metformin significantly inhibited the expression of HIF1α and c-Myc in pathological B cells from women with PCOS.
source: We therefore detected the effect of metformin on the expression of HIF1α and c-Myc in pathological B cells from women with PCOS. The results showed that metformin significantly inhibited the expression of HIF1α and c-Myc (Figure 5G–I).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5G-I.

claim: Rapamycin exhibited a time-dependent inhibitory effect on the expression of TNF-α in pathological B cells from women with PCOS.
source: As expected, rapamycin exhibited a time-dependent inhibitory effect on the expression of TNF-α in pathological B cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Rapamycin decreased the MMP, ROS levels and glucose uptake in pathological B cells from women with PCOS.
source: We also investigated the effects of rapamycin on mitochondrial metabolic state and glucose uptake, and found that rapamycin decreased the MMP, ROS levels and glucose uptake in pathological B cells (Figure 6B–E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6B-E.

claim: mTOR phosphorylation was involved in the inhibitory effect of metformin on the production of TNF-α and metabolic reprogramming of B cells in women with PCOS.
source: These results were consistent with the effect of metformin on pathological B cells, demonstrating that mTOR phosphorylation was involved in the inhibitory effect of metformin on the production of TNF-α and metabolic reprogramming of B cells in women with PCOS.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity between rapamycin and metformin effects.

claim: DHEA-induced PCOS mice had fewer corpora lutea, more cystic follicles, and thicker theca cell layers.
source: DHEA-induced PCOS mice had fewer corpora lutea, more cystic follicles, and thicker theca cell layers, which were consistent with the changes in ovarian morphology in women with PCOS (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: The ovarian morphology changes in DHEA-induced PCOS mice were consistent with the changes in ovarian morphology in women with PCOS.
source: DHEA-induced PCOS mice had fewer corpora lutea, more cystic follicles, and thicker theca cell layers, which were consistent with the changes in ovarian morphology in women with PCOS (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between mouse model and human PCOS.

claim: Estrous cycling was disrupted in PCOS mice as determined by vaginal cytology.
source: In addition, estrous cycling was disrupted in PCOS mice as determined by vaginal cytology (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by estrous cycle data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: After metformin treatment, the PCOS mice showed an increased number of corpora lutea and normal estrous cycles.
source: After metformin treatment, the PCOS mice showed an increased number of corpora lutea and normal estrous cycles (Figure 7B–E).
evidence: This is supported by histological and estrous cycle data shown in Figure 7B-E.

claim: Metformin treatment can reverse ovulatory dysfunction in DHEA-induced PCOS mice.
source: These results suggest that metformin treatment can reverse ovulatory dysfunction in DHEA-induced PCOS mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the restoration of corpora lutea and estrous cycles.

claim: PCOS mice showed impaired glucose tolerance.
source: In the glucose tolerance tests (GTTs), PCOS mice showed impaired glucose tolerance, while metformin could markedly lower glucose levels and GTT area under the curve (GTT AUC), indicating that metformin can restore the impaired glucose tolerance of PCOS mice (Figure 7F–G).
evidence: This is supported by GTT data shown in Figure 7F-G.

claim: Metformin could markedly lower glucose levels and GTT area under the curve (GTT AUC) in PCOS mice.
source: In the glucose tolerance tests (GTTs), PCOS mice showed impaired glucose tolerance, while metformin could markedly lower glucose levels and GTT area under the curve (GTT AUC), indicating that metformin can restore the impaired glucose tolerance of PCOS mice (Figure 7F–G).
evidence: This is supported by GTT data shown in Figure 7F-G.

claim: Metformin can restore the impaired glucose tolerance of PCOS mice.
source: In the glucose tolerance tests (GTTs), PCOS mice showed impaired glucose tolerance, while metformin could markedly lower glucose levels and GTT area under the curve (GTT AUC), indicating that metformin can restore the impaired glucose tolerance of PCOS mice (Figure 7F–G).
evidence: This is inferred from the improvement in GTT shown in Figure 7F-G.

claim: The level of TNF-α was higher in mice with PCOS compared with control subjects.
source: We further detected the level of TNF-α in serum, the results showed that the level of TNF-α was higher in mice with PCOS compared with control subjects, and metformin inhibited this increase (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by serum TNF-α measurements shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Metformin inhibited the increase in serum TNF-α levels in PCOS mice.
source: We further detected the level of TNF-α in serum, the results showed that the level of TNF-α was higher in mice with PCOS compared with control subjects, and metformin inhibited this increase (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is supported by serum TNF-α measurements shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Metformin treatment reverses abnormal ovarian morphology, disturbed estrous cycle, impaired glucose metabolism and abnormal serum TNF-α levels in DHEA-induced PCOS mice.
source: These data suggest that metformin treatment reverses abnormal ovarian morphology, disturbed estrous cycle, impaired glucose metabolism and abnormal serum TNF-α levels in DHEA-induced PCOS mice.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the data presented in Figure 7.

claim: The percentage of TNF-α+ cells in CD19+ B cells was notably higher in mice with PCOS than that in control groups.
source: The percentage of TNF-α+ cells in CD19+ B cells was notably higher in mice with PCOS than that in control groups and metformin inhibited the expression of TNF-α in pathological B cells (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Metformin inhibited the expression of TNF-α in pathological B cells from DHEA-induced PCOS mice.
source: The percentage of TNF-α+ cells in CD19+ B cells was notably higher in mice with PCOS than that in control groups and metformin inhibited the expression of TNF-α in pathological B cells (Figure 8A).
